finding: The live range of $170-$700 is about right at the bottom and generous at the top for a single front door. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2017 Hyundai Elantra about $186-$395 ($114.13-$154.66 parts, 0.6-1.5 hr); midsize 2009 Honda CR-V about $119-$420 ($59.27-$179.70, 0.5-1.5 hr); truck 2017 Ford F-150 about $230-$390 ($109.99-$149.68, 1.0-1.5 hr); luxury 2013 Acura ILX about $99-$341 ($50.81-$100.81, 0.4-1.5 hr). The lowest totals ($99-$119) combine an online aftermarket part with a 0.4-0.5 hour manufacturer warranty time, which is less than a shop normally charges for either, so $170 is a fair floor. The four examples top out near $420, but they were chosen because their makers print a labor time, and three of them have inexpensive genuine latches. Other common cars cost more in parts: a genuine Toyota lock assembly for a 2015 Corolla lists at $365.92 and a genuine BMW F30 latch at $283.59, which at the general 1.5 hours and $160/hr come to about $606 and $524 (those two totals rest on a general labor statement, not a time for those cars). YourMechanic's shop/dealer figure for an Acura TLX tops out near $601 and RepairPal's national average is $381-$484. So $700 is above anything we could build at $160/hr, but it is plausible at a dealer charging more than $160/hr or once diagnosis is added; a ceiling nearer $600-$650 would match the evidence more closely. The Acura ILX shares its latch with Honda models, so it is a cheap luxury example and should not be read as typical of European luxury cars. On all four vehicles the actuator comes as one piece with the door latch. How solid the labor times are: every class now has a low end stated for the example vehicle itself. Three are manufacturer warranty times printed in dealer bulletins: Hyundai 0.6 hr for one door latch on the 2017 Elantra (warranty extension bulletin 21-BD-006H), Honda 0.5 hr for the driver's actuator and 0.6 hr for a front passenger latch assembly on the 2007-09 CR-V, and Honda/Acura 0.4 hr for a front door latch on the 2013 ILX (recall bulletin 12-023). The F-150 low end is a parts seller's 'approx 1 hour', not a book time; a Nissan bulletin gives 0.5 hr for a front door lock assembly on another full-size pickup (2016-2018 Titan), and Ford's own F-150 latch documents print times only for sealing and shield work, not for replacing a latch. Warranty times are the low end of what shops bill. Every high end still rests on one named author's general statement of 0.8-1.5 hours at a dealership; no second stated time for any of the example vehicles was found, so exactly half of the hours figures (the four high ends) are not vehicle-specific and confidence stays low. Parts caveats: the Elantra aftermarket actuator ($114.13) costs slightly more than the genuine latch at a discounted online price ($110.08), so that class is narrow; the Elantra and ILX aftermarket pages do not say in words that the latch is included; the CR-V $59.27 part's page does not say which door it fits (a Dorman front-left latch with actuator for that CR-V is $104.99). An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis. Reviewer note (2026-11-20): the luxury class was put back to the 2015 BMW 328i (0.8-1.5 hr, parts $95.99-$283.59, about $192-$524 built) so the range still covers a European car. Honda's 0.4 hr for the 2013 Acura ILX front door latch (parts $50.81-$100.81) is a cross-check: https://static.nhtsa.gov/odi/rcl/2012/RCRIT-12V338-6677.pdf
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis fee (a lock that will not work can also be a fuse, switch, wiring in the door hinge area, or a control module, not the actuator), shop supplies, and sales tax. Broken door panel clips, a vapor barrier reseal, or a lock rod or cable are sometimes added. Other doors are quoted separately, and when one actuator has failed from age the others often follow. Some vehicles need the new latch programmed or the door ajar and anti-theft functions checked afterward.
